title: Inversion & emphasis
note: negative/limiting adverbials (never, rarely, seldom, little, nowhere, at no time, under no circumstances, in no way, not only, no sooner, hardly) · Only … / Not until … including where the inversion lands when a whole clause is fronted · inverted conditionals had/were/should, plus Had it not been for / Were it not for · so + adj / such + noun with the that-result clause · 4 strands x 12 · 48 items · built to live 2026-08-07 (cloud run 11)

items.en: Never have I seen such a beautiful garden.
items.cz: Nikdy jsem neviděl tak krásnou zahradu.
items.gap: Never ____ such a beautiful garden.
accepts: Never have I seen such a beautiful garden.
items.explanation: When a negative or limiting adverbial is fronted, the subject and the auxiliary swap places, exactly as in a question — but the sentence is a statement. If there is no auxiliary, do / does / did supplies one.
items.explanation_cz: Když se záporné nebo omezující příslovečné určení dostane na začátek věty, podmět a pomocné sloveso si vymění místo přesně jako v otázce — věta ale zůstává oznamovací. Není-li tam pomocné sloveso, dodá ho do / does / did.

items.explanation: Only … and Not until … work the same way, with one trap: when the fronted part is a whole clause, the inversion lands on the main clause that follows, never inside the fronted clause itself.
items.explanation_cz: Only … a Not until … fungují stejně, mají ale jednu past: když je na začátku celá vedlejší věta, inverze se objeví až v následující větě hlavní, nikdy uvnitř té předsunuté.

items.explanation: Formal conditionals drop if and invert instead. Only three verbs do this: had for the third conditional, were for the second, and should for an open future condition. The negative keeps not after the subject: Had it not been for…
items.explanation_cz: Formální podmínkové věty vypouštějí if a místo něj používají inverzi. Dělají to jen tři slovesa: had u třetího kondicionálu, were u druhého a should u otevřené budoucí podmínky. Zápor ponechává not až za podmětem: Had it not been for…

cards.title: Inversion: question order in a statement
cards.title_cz: Inverze: pořádek slov jako v otázce, ale ve větě oznamovací
cards.body: Put certain words at the front of a sentence and English forces the subject and the auxiliary to swap places — the same order as a question, but nothing is being asked. It is a formal, emphatic move, common in writing and in speeches, rare in ordinary conversation.
cards.body_cz: Postavíte-li určitá slova na začátek věty, angličtina vynutí prohození podmětu a pomocného slovesa — stejné pořadí jako v otázce, ale na nic se neptáme. Je to formální a důrazný prostředek, běžný v psaném textu a v projevech, v běžném hovoru vzácný.

table.caption: what triggers it
rows: negative / limiting adverbial
Never have I seen such a beautiful garden.
Only … / Not until …
Only then did I understand the problem.
conditional without if
Had I known about the traffic, I would have left earlier.
so + adjective / such + noun
So difficult was the exam that half the students failed.

points: Normal order: I have never seen such a garden. Inverted: Never have I seen…
If there is no auxiliary, do / does / did appears to carry the inversion.

cards.title: Negative and limiting adverbials
cards.body: These are the words that trigger it: never, rarely, seldom, little, nowhere, at no time, under no circumstances, in no way, not only, no sooner, hardly.
cards.body_cz: Spouštěči jsou tato slova: never, rarely, seldom, little, nowhere, at no time, under no circumstances, in no way, not only, no sooner, hardly.
points: Rarely does he leave the office before eight. (no auxiliary in the plain sentence, so does appears)
Little did she know … is a fixed expression: the speaker knew something the subject did not.
No sooner … than, but Hardly … when — the second half is not interchangeable.
Not only takes a second half with but … also: Not only did she pay for dinner, but she also drove us home.

cards.title: Only … and Not until … — where the inversion lands
cards.title_cz: Only … a Not until … — kam inverze patří
cards.body: This is the one that catches people out. When the fronted part is a whole clause, that clause keeps normal word order and the inversion appears in the main clause that follows.
cards.body_cz: Tady se chybuje nejčastěji. Když je vpředu celá vedlejší věta, ta si ponechá normální pořádek slov a inverze se objeví až ve větě hlavní.

table.caption: the fronted clause keeps normal order
rows: Only after the guests had left
did we start to clean.
Only when the rain stopped
could we walk to the beach.
Not until you have paid
can we send the tickets.

points: ✗ Only after had the guests left, we started to clean.
With a short phrase there is no second clause and it is simpler: Only then did I understand.

cards.title: Conditionals without if
cards.body: Formal English drops if and inverts instead. Only three verbs can do it: had, were and should.
cards.body_cz: Formální angličtina vypouští if a nahrazuje ho inverzí. Umí to jen tři slovesa: had, were a should.

table.caption: the three
rows: If I had known about the traffic…
Had I known about the traffic…
If I lost this job…
Were I to lose this job…
If you need any help…
Should you need any help…

points: The negative keeps not after the subject: Had it not been for your advice…
Were it not for the noise… is the present equivalent of the same thing.
Never contract these: ✗ Hadn't I known. The negative must be written out.

cards.title: so and such
cards.body: Front the quality and the subject and verb invert behind it. so goes with an adjective or an adverb; such goes with a noun. The that-clause gives the result.
cards.body_cz: Předsuňte vlastnost a podmět se slovesem se za ní obrátí. so se pojí s přídavným jménem nebo příslovcem, such s podstatným jménem. Vedlejší věta s that udává následek.

table.caption: so or such
rows: So difficult was the exam that half the students failed.
Such was the noise that we could not work.
So loudly did they argue that the neighbours complained.
Such was his surprise that he could not speak.

points: so many / so much with quantity: So many people came that we had no chairs left.
The verb agrees with what follows it: So impressive were the results…

cards.title: Common mistakes

table.caption: check
rows: Never I have seen such a garden.
Never have I seen such a beautiful garden.
Rarely he leaves the office before eight.
Rarely does he leave the office before eight.
Only after had the guests left, we started to clean.
Only after the guests had left did we start to clean.
If I would have known, I would have left earlier.
Had I known about the traffic, I would have left earlier.
Such difficult was the exam that half the students failed.
So difficult was the exam that half the students failed.
So was the noise that we could not work.
Such was the noise that we could not work.

points: Czech marks emphasis by word order freely; English pays for it with a fixed grammatical swap.
Inversion is formal. Used in a casual email it sounds odd, not clever.
